narrative: A 25-year-old woman arrived on the small Greek island of Nera at about 3:30 a.m. on a cold October morning in 2015, after a long, dark Aegean crossing. Local fishermen helped them ashore, eager to take the boat's valuable engine. She and the other women and children rested in a small room by the beach, but it was too cold to sleep. At first light they walked about two and a half miles to the police station, where hundreds stood in line to register for the onward boat to Kos. When her turn came, the number 17 was written on her hand; she would never forget the day she became just a number on a long, inhuman list. With the registration paper she took a 12-hour ship to Athens, arriving the next morning. That night a Greek friend helped her onto a bus to the Macedonian border, which she reached at 6 a.m. She argued with an unfair border guard who was letting new arrivals ahead of people who had waited longer; he told her, 'You seem nervous. If you want, you can go back to your country and stay there.' A friend calmed her down. They paid 25 euros each to board an old, filthy train she compared to a walking trash pile, which moved, as Syrians say of slow things, as if walking on eggs. She reached the Serbian border, then walked about four miles to a registration town she cannot name. There refugees were kept in the streets, allowed inside only briefly to be turned into a number, treated badly by the Serbian police; some she met had been sleeping in the street for days waiting for a paper. A Serbian journalist helped her get through faster and arranged a few hours on a bus to Croatia, where she was met with real compassion, hot tea and rest. The same day she took a train to Hungary, where she saw the new border fences that would close only a week after her arrival. A few hours later she was in Vienna, sleeping in a sports complex turned into a refugee shelter. In the morning she booked a ticket to Germany, terrified of being caught at Passau on the Austrian border. On the train she spoke no Arabic, to hide that she was a refugee, and chatted with two American tourists who complained about refugees without knowing she was one. At the border German police boarded and she pretended to sleep for half an hour; migrants around her were caught and taken off, but she was not spotted - perhaps, she thought, because she spoke some English and wore no hijab. As the doors closed she opened her eyes from her fake sleep to see rows of people standing with police around them, like criminals. That was her first experience of Germany. She settled in a tiny northern town near the Netherlands, awaiting a three-year visa so she could move to Berlin and rejoin her husband.
